extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and scholars of narratology, literary critics, and advanced readers of fiction theory
extracted.subtask_description: Close analytic reading of narrative discourse focusing on temporal organization, mood (distance/perspective), and modes of reporting speech (diegesis vs mimesis, narrated vs narrated words). Intended to guide theoretical description and critical evaluation of novels and narrative technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequence & Frequency (order vs frequency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Connects chronological succession with frequency: narratives may present events in chronological order or rearrange them; frequency (especially the iterative) often dominates in memory-driven passages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Proust's initial sections are 'mainly iterative plateaux' (childhood in Combray, Swann's love, Gilberte) where repetition masks passage of time. Memory reduces diachronic periods to synchronic epochs and events to pictures; hence sequence (order) and frequency (iteration/singulation) must be evaluated together when analyzing temporal organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anachronism as product of memory
rubrics_metrics.description: Anachronism (voluntary or involuntary) in narrative arises from the work of memory and should be read as a memory-effect rather than mere chronological error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genette: 'The anachronism of the memories ... and their static nature are obviously in league with each other in that they both arise from the work of memory.' Evaluate instances of anachrony by considering whether they enact memory's non-chronological laws rather than failing chronological fidelity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dominance of iterative vs singulative across narrative phases
rubrics_metrics.description: The balance between iterative (repetition) and singulative (unique scenes) modes can shift across a work, correlating with changes in the presence of the remembering instance and the emancipation of 'story' from 'narrative'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in Proust, early sections show iterative dominance tied to the intermediary subject's memory; later Balbec–Guermantes series restores chronological order and singulative scenes as the remembering instance fades, changing the narrative's temporal texture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distortions of duration (ellipses and monstrous scenes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative duration can be distorted by enormous ellipses and disproportionately long scenes; such distortions affect how time is perceived in the story-world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These distortions may come from the narrator (e.g., impatience, desire to load final scenes) rather than the intermediary subject. Identify ellipses and extended scenes, and assess whether they function to compress or expand perceived duration and to what narrative end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporality of the narrating instance (narrating time)
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrating itself has a temporality that can govern and distort the narrative (distinct from diegetic temporality); the narrator's temporal impulses (e.g., urgency to reach denouement) shape the text's temporal organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genette notes the narrator may 'load his final scenes ... and jump to the denouement' — evaluate how narrative pacing and final-stage accelerations reflect the narrating instance's temporal aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpolations, distortions, temporal condensations (three kinds of temporal distortion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three main kinds of temporal distortion affect order, duration, or frequency: interpolations (anachronies), alternation scenes/ellipses (duration distortions), and iterative syllepsis (condensing several events into one narrative instance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these categories to classify temporal phenomena: Proust admired Balzac's 'interpolations'; iterative syllepsis condenses events; alternation of scenes and ellipses distorts duration. Explicitly map observed distortions to these three types when analyzing temporal structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial/realistic justification for temporal distortions
rubrics_metrics.description: Temporal distortions are often justified (by the author within the text or by critical rationalization) as attempts to tell things as they were 'lived' or as they were 'recalled'; such motivations may be aesthetic rather than documentary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genette cautions the analyst not to be satisfied with retrospective rationalizations: evaluate whether the justification (subjective memory vs objective demonstration) functions as an aesthetic medium in the work rather than taking it at face value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memory as compositional device / method of transition
rubrics_metrics.description: Involuntary memory and remembered phenomena can serve as significant compositional links and methods of transition between narrative planes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the madeleine functions as a 'significant link' and method of sudden transition in Proust. When encountering abrupt transitions, assess whether they are motivated compositionally by memory phenomena rather than arbitrary cuts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Showing vs telling (mimesis vs diegesis) framed as information + informer
rubrics_metrics.description: The mimetic (showing) vs diegetic (telling) distinction can be usefully formalized: information + informer = constant; mimesis is characterized by maximal information and minimal presence of the informer (narrator), while diegesis is the opposite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the formula 'information + informer = C' when judging passages: high-detail scenes with vanishing narrator presence create mimetic illusion; overt commentary reduces mimesis. Note Genette's caveat that 'showing' is only a way of telling—no narrative literally imitates the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative mood as regulation of information: distance and perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative 'mood' (extended from grammatical mood) designates degrees of informational affirmation and the regulation of narrative information according to distance (how far narrator stands from story) and perspective (point of view adopted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'distance' to diagnose mediation vs directness, and 'perspective' to identify whose vision filters information. Recognize mood as the mechanisms by which the narrative controls amount, directness, and point-of-view of delivered information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship between narrative speed and quantity of information
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantity of narrative information is in inverse ratio to narrative speed: more information (detailed scene) implies slower narrative pace; less information implies acceleration or ellipsis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When mapping narrative time, correlate dense, mimetic passages with slow pacing and ellipses/summary with rapid pacing. This relation also ties to perceived immediacy and the mimetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textual features that create mimetic illusion (details as connotators of mimesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain textual details (even functionally 'useless' ones) act as connotators of mimesis, producing the referential illusion that the narrative 'shows' rather than 'tells'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Homeric 'shore of the loud-sounding sea' is a 'useless and contingent detail' that produces a realistic effect. Identify such contingent details as deliberate devices to heighten the illusion of showing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative of events vs narrative of words (limits of mimesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mimesis of non-verbal events is always an illusion—narration transcribes nonverbal into verbal; by contrast, reporting words (dialogue, inner speech) admits different regimes (recopying, narratization) with different mimetic stakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing apparent imitation, distinguish whether the object is events (always mediated) or words (which may be literally reproduced). Plato's rewritings illustrate how speech becomes event under narratization and reduces mimesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three/four degrees of reporting speech (narratized, transposed/indirect, free indirect, quoted/direct)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters' speech (uttered or inner) can appear in at least three states: (1) narratized/narrated (most distant/reduced), (2) transposed/indirect (acknowledged narrator mediation), (3) free indirect (blend & ambiguity between narrator and character), and (4) quoted/direct (most mimetic/dramatic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these categories diagnostically: narratized = 'I informed my mother'; transposed = 'I told her that...'; free indirect = absence of declarative verb and syntactic markings producing ambiguity; quoted/direct = 'I said, "..."' Evaluate how each state affects perceived immediacy, narrator presence, and ideological stance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free indirect style as tool of ambiguity/emancipation
rubrics_metrics.description: Free indirect style economizes on subordination and allows a greater extension of character speech while producing ambiguity between uttered/inner speech and between character voice and narrator voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess free indirect passages for their deliberate double confusion: (a) between thought and utterance, (b) between character language and narrator's language. Note Genette's point that Flaubert used this to make 'the other' speak in the narrator's language without fully compromising the narrator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrator's presence as analyst, commentator, stylist and its paradoxical coexistence with mimetic illusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Even in works with intense mimetic passages, the narrator often remains a present source, organizer, and stylist (producer of metaphors and commentary); high mediation and high immediacy can coexist paradoxically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Proust's passages are both 'extreme mediation' and 'utmost immediacy.' When evaluating a passage's mimesis, attend to how narrator commentary, analysis, or metaphorical framing coexists with scene-like descriptions.
